# HP 2000F and HP 2000 Access Time-Shared BASIC

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

Author: Thomas Dzubin    License: MIT    Version: see `VERSION` in
[`hp2000f_const.h`](hp2000f_const.h) and
[`hp2000access_const.h`](hp2000access_const.h)

**Status:** the main system is **HP 2000 Access**. It runs the most programs from
the HP contributed library (1054 of them are installed in its system library, on a
24 MB 2883 disc) and works on the PicoCalc. The **2000F** is kept as well, as the
system the author used in the 1970s; it is built and tested on a PC and has not
been run on a PicoCalc yet. The first version, the one-CPU **2000E**, has been
archived in [`archive/hp2000e/`](archive/hp2000e/) (source and constants); to build it again, move `hp2000e.c` and `hp2000e_const.h`
back and add an E branch to the two `CMakeLists.txt` files. The project is called
`hp2000tsb` because it has emulated all three Time-Shared BASIC (TSB) systems.

An emulator of the Hewlett-Packard 2100 minicomputer that runs the real **HP 2000
Time-Shared BASIC** system of the 1970s on the ClockworkPi **PicoCalc**
(Raspberry Pi Pico 2), also buildable for Windows and Linux. The operating system
is loaded from the SD card, and the SD card is also the disc and tape storage, so
programs you save in BASIC survive a power-off.

It is written in plain C. The CPU, the floating point firmware and the devices
follow the HP 2100 simulator in the SIMH project (see Credits), and every part
was checked against a reference build of SIMH.

## A little history

The HP 2000 was Hewlett-Packard's family of time-sharing BASIC systems of 1968 to 1978,
built on its 2100-series 16-bit minicomputers; it was the first minicomputer to offer
time-shared BASIC, and HP's library of customer-written programs is where the first
published versions of *Star Trek* came from. The longer story, with sources, is in
[`docs/HISTORY.md`](docs/HISTORY.md).

## What it emulates

Two HP 2100 computers with 32K words each, running side by side (the 2000F and
Access are two-computer systems):

- the **System Processor** runs the BASIC interpreter and has the extended
  arithmetic unit, the floating point firmware, a 12565A disc interface with an
  HP 2883 drive (24 MB), a 13183B magnetic tape controller (HIBERNATE and reload),
  a teleprinter for the operator console, a time base generator and the DMA;
- the **I/O Processor** (with the 2000 IOP instruction set on Access) runs the
  12920A terminal multiplexer for the user terminals;
- a 12875A Processor Interconnect joins the two.

You get two terminals on the PicoCalc's screen, switched with a key, and a
second, independent user terminal over the USB cable:

- **Operator console** (F1): where TSB asks its start-up questions and prints
  its system messages.
- **User terminal** (F2): the PicoCalc's keyboard and screen as a TSB terminal.
- **USB terminal**: any serial terminal program on a PC (PuTTY, Tera Term,
  `screen`) can log on as another user at the same time.

## What you need

- A PicoCalc with a Pico 2 (RP2350) and a FAT32 formatted SD card.
- The system's files in a folder on the card: `/hp2000access/` for Access,
  `/hp2000f/` for the 2000F. They come in two zip files on the release page,
  `hp2000access-data.zip` and `hp2000f-data.zip`, each holding the folder to copy
  to the top level of the card (or to put next to the Windows program).
  **`HOW-TO-RUN.txt` lists exactly which files go where**, for the PicoCalc and
  for Windows.

**About the files in those zips.** They are Hewlett-Packard's operating system
(TSB, the HP 2000 Access and 2000F systems) and the contributed library programs of
HP's user group, in the form of a disc image and tapes made with the SIMH project's
kits (`2000-Access-kit-release-6.zip`, `2000F-kit-release-7.zip` and
`2000E-kit-release-4.zip` at <http://simh.trailing-edge.com/hp/>) and the library
tape on Bitsavers. They belong to Hewlett-Packard and the program authors and are
**not licensed with this project** (the MIT License covers only this project's own code
and documents); they are offered here, as the SIMH kits are, for hobby and historical
use, so that the emulator can be tried. The disc is made by the test session program
(`genaccess`, `genf` in `tests/`) and the library import. If you are the owner of
rights in any of it and want it taken down, say so in an issue.

## The 2000F (a second, separate system)

The same program family also builds an emulator of the **HP 2000F** (rev 1410), a
two-computer system: a System Processor (32K words) runs the BASIC interpreter
and has the disc, the tape and the operator console, and an I/O Processor (8K
words) runs the terminal multiplexer. The 2000F and Access are separate
builds with their own program (`hp2000f.c`, `hp2000access.c`), their own constants
and their own SD card folder, so either can be built without the other:

| | 2000F | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Program | `hp2000f.c` | `hp2000access.c` |
| Build | `-DHP_SYSTEM=F` (firmware and desktop) | `-DHP_SYSTEM=ACCESS` (the default) |
| Output | `hp2000f-RP2350.uf2` | `hp2000access-RP2350.uf2` |
| SD folder | `/hp2000f/` | `/hp2000access/` |
| Files there | `SYSTEM-2883.disc`, `HIBERNATE-2883.tape`, `24343-60001_Rev-1710.abin`, `24339-60001_Rev-1710.abin` (the two paper tapes are from the SIMH 2000F kit; the disc and tape come from the generation described below) | see the Access section below |
| Shut down | F4: H HIBERNATE, S SLEEP, D SLEEP + tape | F4: H HIBERNATE, S SLEEP, D SLEEP + tape |

The 2000F has the same menu, title screen, spare copies, SD diagnostics and 6 MHz card clock
as Access. Its start-up asks `CONFIGURATION OPTIONS?` (the program answers `NO`), then the
date and time (you give them on the menu, as on Access, and the program types them), and
the program types the tape select code once the system says `READY`. Its SLEEP and its
recovery were confirmed on a PicoCalc with an earlier build; the build with the menu date
and time, the spare copies and the SD fixes has been run on a PC only (reload, SLEEP,
restart, SLEEP with a tape dump, restore, HIBERNATE) and not yet on a PicoCalc.

## HP 2000 Access (a third, separate system)

**HP 2000 Access** (rev 1812) is the later two-computer system. Both computers are
HP 2100s with 32K words; the I/O Processor has the 2000 IOP instruction set
(`hp21xx_iop.c`). It accepts statements and strings up to 255 characters and the
extra syntax of the HP library programs (49 of 62 games from the contributed
library were accepted, against 17 on the 2000F). It is its own program,
`hp2000access.c` with `hp2000access_const.h`, built with `-DHP_SYSTEM=ACCESS`
(`hp2000access-RP2350.uf2`, `hp2000access-Windows.exe`) and reads its files from
`/hp2000access/` on the SD card:

- `SYSTEM-2883.disc`, the system disc, 23,905,280 bytes: a 2883 drive of about 24 MB on a 12565A interface (made by the kit's own generation procedure,
  see `docs/TSB-LIBRARY.md`)
- `HIBERNATE-2883.tape`, written at every HIBERNATE (F4, H)
- `SLEEP-2883.tape`, written by F4, D (created when first needed)
- `IOP-2100.tape`, the I/O Processor's program and its cross-loader
- `22687-11002_Rev-1812.tape`, the Master Control Program (needed by the R reload only)

The system disc and tape that come with the kit are not slept, so the first time
(and after any bad shutdown) start with **R**, which reloads the system from the
HIBERNATE tape. After a good F4 shutdown start with **B**. The program first asks
for the date (`DAY/YY`, for example `281/26`) and the time (`HHMM`, for example
`1200`) and types the answers to the system's `DATE?` and `TIME?` for you. When the
banner `HP22687A-1812` appears, press F2 for the user terminal and press RETURN
once: the multiplexer sends the line feed that the log-in handshake needs after
the first carriage return, and `PLEASE LOG IN` comes back. Log on with
`HELLO-B001,RICK`. F4 does a HIBERNATE (it answers the questions itself) and the
menu comes back when the tape is written. It has run on a PicoCalc (RP2350) as well
as on a PC.

## Windows display

The Windows and Linux programs show the terminals 80 characters wide: their screen is 640 x 320 pixels instead of the
PicoCalc's 320 x 320 (`desktop/wide/lcd.h` changes only `WIDTH`, the vendored header is untouched), drawn with the same
8 x 10 pixel font, and the window opens at twice that size (about 1280 x 640). The PicoCalc keeps 40 columns. The font
has lower case letters; the terminals pass them through (TSB converts commands to capitals by itself, and strings keep
their case). See `HOW-TO-RUN.txt` for what to copy where.

## The contributed library (Access)

The Access system on the SD card has the HP contributed library in the system library (account A000): 1054 programs,
mostly games, statistics, engineering and business programs. From any account:

- `LIBRARY` lists them (a `U` after the name means anyone may use it).
- `GET-$AMAZE` loads one into your work space (`GET-$name` for any name), then `LIST` or `RUN`.
- A program you `SAVE` yourself is private to your account; `UNR-name` makes it available to everyone.

The programs came from the Bitsavers copy of the 1980 library tape. Its listing had lost the dummy variable of every
`DEF FN` statement, and some lines are longer than the 119 characters a terminal line holds; both were repaired by rule
(`tests/tools/repair_library.py` and `fix_long_lines.py`, every change is logged). Not included: `DECSN` (its source is
damaged), `GTAPID` (one very long line) and two files that are data, not programs. The system's disc is a 24 MB 2883
drive; the first start after copying the files is **B** (the disc is already shut down properly), and **F4** shuts down
and writes `HIBERNATE-2883.tape`.

The SD card now and then refuses a write. The program retries and counts these (`SD FAILS n` on the title screen, `[SD ERROR ...]`
on the operator console during a long HIBERNATE); a few per hibernate are normal.

## Using it

The keys are the same on the 2000F and Access (the exact start-up steps for each are in the two system sections above and in `HOW-TO-RUN.txt`).

1. Start the program. A title screen says "PRESS ANY KEY TO START" (ESC or Q leaves for the
   loader); nothing is done to the SD card until a key is pressed. The menu then offers **B** (start the system), **R** (reload
   from the HIBERNATE tape), ESC or Q (back to the UF2 Loader).
2. Press **B**. The program asks for the date (`DAY/YY`, for example `281/26`) and
   the time (`HHMM`) and types the answers to TSB's `DATE?` and `TIME?` for you.
   The PicoCalc has no clock, so this comes up at every start. The operator
   console (F1) shows TSB starting.
3. When the console shows `READY` (Access: the banner `HP22687A-1812`), press **F2**
   for the user terminal and log on with one of the accounts that ship with the
   system: `HELLO-A000,OZZIE`, `HELLO-A001,HARIET`, `HELLO-B000,DAVID` or
   `HELLO-B001,RICK`. On Access press RETURN once first (see above). `GET-$AMAZE`
   then `RUN` loads and runs a library program (Access).
4. TSB's character delete is the underscore; **Backspace** types it for you.
   Line delete is CTRL+X. Lower case letters are passed through; TSB turns
   commands into capitals itself.

### Importing and exporting text without a serial cable (F6 and F7)

A text file on the SD card can be typed into the user terminal, and what the user
terminal prints can be saved to a text file on the card. Both work while the system runs
and are the same on the 2000F and Access, on the PicoCalc and on Windows and Linux.

**Import (F6).** Log in on the user terminal (F2) and press **F6**. A list of the `.TXT`
and `.BAS` files in the system's SD folder appears (the program's own `RUNLOG.TXT` and
checksum files are left out); **Up** and **Down** choose, **Enter** starts, **ESC** cancels.
The machine waits while the list is shown. The program then types the file into the user
terminal one line at a time, exactly as you would at the keyboard: it sends a line, waits
for TSB's echo of the line feed, then gives TSB a short time to finish the line before the
next. The status line shows `IMPORT n OF m  F6 STOPS`; press **F6** again, or BREAK, to stop.
When it is finished the status line says how many lines were sent and how many TSB refused
(it prints `???` for a line it does not accept). Keys you type meanwhile are ignored, so they
cannot mix with the file.

What TSB makes of the file is up to TSB: **a file is only a list of lines to type.** TSB has
no plain text files, so each line must be something TSB accepts: a numbered BASIC line, or a
command. A file that makes and keeps a program can therefore look like this:

```
SCR
10 PRINT "HELLO"
20 PRINT 6*7
30 END
NAME-HELLO
SAVE
```

`SCR` clears the workspace, the numbered lines become the program in memory (so `RUN` works
at once), and `NAME-HELLO` with `SAVE` writes it to the disc as a TSB program file. A line
longer than 119 characters is cut, empty lines are skipped, and a tab becomes a space.
Data files (the kind a program opens with `FILES`) are not programs, so they cannot be
made by typing text; a BASIC program in the import can write one.

**Export (F7).** Press **F7** to start copying everything the user terminal prints into
`EXPORT.TXT` in the system's SD folder, and press **F7** again to stop. A `LIST`, a `RUN`
or anything else printed between the two presses is saved. The text is added after
what the file already holds (a new file is made if there is none), and the file is cut to
its exact length when you stop, so it holds no padding. Lines end in carriage return and line
feed, as TSB prints them. The status line shows `CAPTURING TO EXPORT.TXT  F7 STOPS`.

### Spare copies (menu V, X and W)

The disc and the HIBERNATE tape change with every run, and a bad shutdown leaves
"SYSTEM NOT SLEPT". The program keeps two spare sets of `SYSTEM-2883.disc` and
`HIBERNATE-2883.tape` in the same folder, in two slots used in turn: `SP1F0.BIN` and
`SP1F1.BIN` with `SP1SUMS.TXT` (slot 1), and `SP2F0.BIN`, `SP2F1.BIN`, `SP2SUMS.TXT` (slot 2).
The `SUMS.TXT` file holds a sequence number and each file's size and CRC-32; it is written
last, so a slot counts only if its copy finished and read back correctly. The slot with the
higher sequence number is the newest spare.

- **V** saves a new spare into the older slot (it asks first). The newest spare is never
  touched, so a failure or a power cut cannot leave you without a good spare. Each file is
  copied, then read back and checked. V is refused while the last run is marked as not clean.
- **X** restores the newest spare, **W** the older one (each asks first). The spare is first
  read back and checked against its checksums; if it is damaged nothing is changed. Then the live
  files are replaced and checked again. The SLEEP tape, which no longer matches the restored
  disc, is deleted.
- After a clean HIBERNATE the program offers to save a spare at once (the best moment to take one).
- **Unclean-shutdown note:** `SESSION.FLG` says R while the machine runs and C after a clean
  HIBERNATE or SLEEP (or a restore). If the program starts and finds R, the menu says "LAST RUN
  DID NOT END CLEANLY" and points to R or S (reload) or X (restore).
- At start-up, if there are no spares at all (and the last run was clean), they are saved from
  the live files before the menu appears, with the progress on screen. If some are there but no
  slot is complete, the menu says so and leaves them alone.

Saving the 24 MB disc and the tape takes about two minutes on the PicoCalc (copy, then read back).
Nothing is ever renamed or edited in place, and the spares use plain 8.3 names, because the FAT32
driver's directory code is fragile (see `docs/fat32-pr/PULL-REQUEST.md`).

### Shutting down: always use F4

TSB must be shut down properly before the power goes off. **F4** asks on the status
line which kind of shutdown, and answers the system's questions for you. Log all
users off (`BYE`) first.

- **H, HIBERNATE:** the whole system and every program and file are written to the
  HIBERNATE tape on the SD card (`SYSTEM HIBERNATED`, `TAPE WRITTEN`). Slow, and many
  SD writes. HP recommends it once a week.
- **S, SLEEP:** the system is written back onto the disc only (`SYSTEM SLEPT. START
  WITH B.`). Quick, no tape. The next start is **B**. On the 2000F the program first
  tells TSB the tape unit is gone (`MAGTAPE-0`) so that the SLEEP does not need a tape.
- **D, SLEEP and tape:** the same, and the programs and files created or changed since
  the last HIBERNATE are also dumped to `SLEEP-2883.tape` (`SYSTEM SLEPT. SLEEP TAPE
  WRITTEN.`). The file is overwritten each time. HP's scheme: SLEEP every day,
  HIBERNATE every week.

When the menu comes back it is safe to power off.

### If the system was not shut down

Starting a system that was not hibernated ends in a halt message (TSB's "SYS NOT
SLEPT"). To recover, press **R** at the menu. The Master Control Program (Access)
or the loader (2000F) reads the HIBERNATE tape and rebuilds the disc from it, then
TSB starts. You answer the date and time as usual. You lose what was changed since
the last HIBERNATE. After a reload the tape drive is off line; press **F3** (ON
LINE) before the next shutdown if TSB asks you to change the tape to AUTO.

If the last shutdown was a SLEEP with a tape (**D**) and the disc cannot be used, press
**S** at the menu instead. On Access it reloads the HIBERNATE tape and then RESTOREs
everything on `SLEEP-2883.tape` over it (the program types `RESTORE`, `ALL` and answers
the tape-features question), so you get back to the state of the last SLEEP. On the
2000F it reads `SLEEP-2883.tape` as the first (most recent) tape set. Both were tested on
a PC by saving a program, SLEEPing, and recovering it. Not yet tried on a PicoCalc.

### The run log

After every run (start, reload, SLEEP, HIBERNATE or a halt) the program appends one line to `RUNLOG.TXT` in the system's folder on the
SD card, so a half hour HIBERNATE needs no one to watch it: how it ended, the seconds, the millions of emulated instructions per second
(MIPS), the seconds spent in SD transfers, the number of transfers and the failed tries. The same figures show under the message on the
menu. The `T` key tests the card's speed in a few seconds. The SD clock is 12 MHz (`STORAGE_PICO_SPI_HZ` in `storage_pico_const.h`).

### The USB terminal

Connect the PicoCalc's USB port to a PC. It appears as a serial port (`COMx` on
Windows, `/dev/ttyACMx` on Linux); the speed setting does not matter. Turn
local echo and local line editing off in the terminal program, because TSB echoes
what you type. **Connect after the system has printed `READY`**: keys typed
before are lost. Log on as a different account from the one on the screen. Ctrl+C
is BREAK; Backspace and Delete are the character delete.

## Controls

| Key | Where | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `B` | menu | starts the system |
| `R` | menu | reloads the system from the HIBERNATE tape |
| `T` | menu | SD speed test (reads 1 MB, writes 256 KB; shows KB/s and failed tries, and logs them) |
| `S` | menu | reloads from the SLEEP tape (Access: HIBERNATE tape first, then RESTORE of the SLEEP tape; 2000F: the SLEEP tape) |
| `ESC` or `Q` | menu | leaves for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu (on a PC it closes) |
| `~` (SHIFT + backtick) | menu only | reboots into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode; while the system runs it is an ordinary key, so a slip cannot lose the session |
| `F1` / `F2` | running | show the operator console / the user terminal |
| `F3` | running | the tape drive's ON LINE button |
| `F4` | running | asks which shutdown: `H` HIBERNATE (whole system to the HIBERNATE tape), `S` SLEEP (system back onto the disc only), `D` SLEEP and dump the entries changed since the last HIBERNATE to `SLEEP-2883.tape`; ESC cancels |
| `BRK` or `F5` | running | BREAK on the terminal being shown |
| `F6` | running | import: choose a `.TXT` or `.BAS` file on the card and type it into the user terminal; `F6` again stops it |
| `F7` | running | start or stop saving what the user terminal prints in `EXPORT.TXT` |
| `Backspace` | running | TSB's character delete (underscore) |
| CTRL + letter | running | the control character |

The PicoCalc screen is 40 columns wide, so TSB's 72 character lines wrap (the Windows and Linux builds show 80 columns). The bottom row
is a status line (F1 and F2 mark the terminal being shown, and show `!` when the
other one has printed something new).

## Files

```
hp2000f.c, hp2000f_const.h  the 2000F program (menu, run loop, keyboard, screen) and all its constants
dev_ipl.c, hp_pair.c        the Processor Interconnect and the running of two CPUs side by side (2000F)
hp_loaders.c                the I/O Processor binary loader, the tape loader and the 7900 and 2883 disc bootstraps (2000F, Access)
hp2000access.c, _const.h    the Access program, the same for two bigger computers
spare.c, .h, _const.h         spare copies of the disc and tape and the restore (menu V and X)
hostfile.c, .h, _const.h      typing a file into the user terminal, and capturing its output (F6 and F7)
hp21xx_iop.c                the 2000 IOP instruction set (Access I/O Processor)
hp21xx.c, .h, _const.h      the HP 2100 CPU, interrupt system and I/O (cards plug in by select code)
hp21xx_fp.c, _fp_const.h    the floating point firmware and extended arithmetic
hp_dma.c, .h, _const.h      the two DMA channels
dev_ptr.c                   paper tape reader (loads the bootstrap and loader)
dev_tty.c                   teleprinter, the operator console
dev_disc.c                  13210A disc controller and the 7900 drive (the 2000E, archived)
dev_dq.c                    12565A disc interface and the 2883 drive (about 24 MB; 2000F and Access)
dev_mux.c                   12920A terminal multiplexer (the user terminals)
dev_tbg.c                   time base generator
dev_tape.c, tape_image.c    13183B tape controller and the SIMH tape image format
console.h                   how the machine's terminals reach the keyboard and screen
storage.h                   how the machine's images reach files
storage_pico.c              storage.h on the SD card (see below)
storage_stdio.c             storage.h on ordinary files (desktop and tests)
platform.h                  the whole interface to the machine: clock, sleep, USB, BOOTSEL
platform_pico.c             platform.h on the Pico SDK
terminal.c, autotype.c      the scrolling terminal and the script that answers the operator questions
termdraw.c                  draws one terminal row on the LCD (40 columns on the PicoCalc, 80 on the desktop)
desktop/                    Desktop (SDL2) build for Windows and Linux (desktop/wide/lcd.h gives the 640 pixel wide screen)
tests/                      host test programs that boot and use the system (tsb_session.c is the main one), the
                            simulated SD card (tests/sdsim/), and the tools used to compare with SIMH and to repair the library
docs/                       research notes, LESSONS-LEARNED.md, TSB-LIBRARY.md, A000-LIBRARY.md (one line per library program)
HOW-TO-RUN.txt              exactly which files go where, for each build
archive/hp2000e/            the archived one-CPU 2000E program (source and constants)
```

Each hardware and operating system dependency sits behind `console.h`,
`storage.h` or `platform.h`, so the emulator code itself is portable C.

### How the SD card is used

`storage_pico.c` includes the FAT32 driver's source (`fat32.c`) so that it can
use the driver's sector functions. The driver itself finds a position in a file by
following the file's cluster chain from the start on every read and write, which
makes a 4.9 MB disc image unusably slow. The storage layer reads each image's
chain once when it is opened and then goes straight to the sector. A write that
makes a file longer (the tape image) still goes through the driver.

The card now and then refuses a sector write, which the driver reports as a failure
at once (TSB then prints `TAPE BAD` at the end of HIBERNATE). Every sector transfer
is therefore tried up to five times, with a short pause and a restart of the card
part way. Each failed try is counted: the Access program prints it on the operator
console as `[SD ERROR n: W S99366 E4]` (read or write, SD sector, driver code; 4 is
a failed write) and shows `SD FAILS n LAST ...` on the menu after a run.

## Building

### With the Raspberry Pi Pico VS Code extension (easiest)

Open this folder, pick the board (Pico 2) and press Compile.

### From a terminal

Set `PICO_SDK_PATH` to your Pico SDK checkout (SDK 2.2.0), then:

```bash
cmake -B build-rp2350-access -G Ninja -DPICO_BOARD=pico2 -DHP_SYSTEM=ACCESS
ninja -C build-rp2350-access
```

(Use `-DHP_SYSTEM=F` and a folder such as `build-rp2350-f` for the 2000F.) The
result is **`hp2000access-RP2350.uf2`** (or `hp2000f-RP2350.uf2`), also copied to
this folder. The RP2040
(`-DPICO_BOARD=pico`) was tried on 2026-10-09 and does not link: the 264 KB of RAM is too small
for the emulated memories plus the program, which now runs from RAM (Access needs about 285 KB).

### On Windows

A small SDL2 layer in [`desktop/`](desktop/) stands in for the PicoCalc's LCD,
keyboard and audio drivers. From an MSYS2 UCRT64 shell with SDL2 installed:

```bash
cmake -S desktop -B build-windows-access -G Ninja -DHP_SYSTEM=ACCESS
ninja -C build-windows-access
```

The result is **`hp2000access-Windows.exe`** (or `hp2000f-Windows.exe` with
`-DHP_SYSTEM=F`) in this folder (SDL2 is linked statically, so it is a single
file). Start it from a folder that holds a `hp2000access` (or `hp2000f`) folder
with the system's files. The PC keyboard takes the place of
the PicoCalc's. The desktop builds have no USB terminal.

### Linux

With the SDL2 development package installed (for example `libsdl2-dev`):

```bash
cmake -S desktop -B build-linux -DHP_SYSTEM=ACCESS
cmake --build build-linux
```

The result is **`hp2000access-Linux`** (or `hp2000f-Linux`) plus **`libSDL2-2.0.so.0`** in this folder.
Keep the two files together; the executable finds the library beside itself.
The Linux build has not been compiled yet.

## Flashing

Press `~` at the menu, or hold BOOTSEL while powering the PicoCalc on. A drive
appears; copy the `.uf2` file onto it.

## Testing

`tests/tsb_session.c` is the main host test: a script-driven session that can
generate a system (`genaccess`, `genf`), boot or reload it, log on, import the
contributed library, hibernate and reload from the tape, for Access or the 2000F
(options and commands are in the file's header). `tests/sdsim/` runs the SD
storage layer on a simulated card with injected write failures (see its
`README.txt`). `tests/test_boot.c` is the original 2000E boot test. `tests/tools/`
holds the library repair scripts and the scripts used to compare instruction
traces and memory dumps with a SIMH reference build. `docs/LESSONS-LEARNED.md` collects what
went wrong and what worked, for anyone who wants to try the same project.

### SIMH

The biggest debt of this project is to **SIMH**, the multi-system simulator
([simh.trailing-edge.com](http://simh.trailing-edge.com/)), and to the authors of its
HP 2100 simulator, **Robert M. Supnik** and **J. David Bryan** (SIMH is under the MIT
license). This program is a new, small C implementation for a microcontroller, but its
behaviour was taken from their work and checked against a reference build of SIMH:

- **Instruction decoding and execution** of the HP 2100 (memory reference, alter/skip,
  shift/rotate, extended arithmetic, I/O and the interrupt rules), from `hp2100_cpu.c`
  and `hp2100_cpu1.c`: `hp21xx.c`.
- **The floating point firmware** (FAD, FSB, FMP, FDV, FIX, FLT, quirks included), from
  `hp2100_cpu_fp.c`: `hp21xx_fp.c`.
- **The I/O Processor instructions** used by the 2000F and Access systems, and the
  Processor Interconnect that joins the two CPUs: `hp21xx_iop.c`, `dev_ipl.c`.
- **The devices:** the 13210A/7900 disc (`dev_disc.c`), the 12565A/2883 disc (`dev_dq.c`),
  the 13183B/7970 magnetic tape (`dev_tape.c`), the 12920A multiplexer (`dev_mux.c`), DMA
  (`hp_dma.c`), the teleprinter, paper tape reader and time base generator cards
  (`dev_tty.c`, `dev_ptr.c`, `dev_tbg.c`), and the loader words (`ipl_loader_const.h`,
  `ptr_loader_const.h`, `hp_loaders.c`).
- **The SIMH tape image format**, read and written by `tape_image.c`.
- **The HP 2000F and Access kits** (loader tapes, system tapes and the instructions for
  generating a system, plus the 2000E kit for the archived system) are distributed from the
  SIMH HP page. The SIMH source used as the reference (HP2100 release 32) and its
  documentation are on that site; they are not copied into this repository.

Without SIMH there would have been no way to know that the emulation was right: the
instruction traces and memory dumps in `tests/tools/` were compared with it.

### Bitsavers

**[Bitsavers](http://www.bitsavers.org/)** (the Software Preservation Group's archive of
old computer software and documentation) supplied the other half of the material:

- **The HP 2000 Contributed Library tape** (`36600-10001`), the source of the 1054 programs
  in the Access system library (see `docs/TSB-LIBRARY.md`), and the other tape images and
  the TSB E and F source listings described there.
- **The scanned HP manuals** (the 2000F and Access BASIC and operator manuals, Access
  internals, the contributed library documentation and more) at
  <https://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/hp/2000TSB/>. They are not copied into this repository.

Thanks to everyone who scanned, read and preserved those tapes and manuals.

HP 2000 TSB (2000E, 2000F and Access), its loaders and the disc and tape images belong to Hewlett-Packard

### Third-party

`picocalc-text-starter-main/` is a vendored copy of
[**picocalc-text-starter**](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter)
by Blair Leduc (the LCD, audio, south-bridge keyboard and SD card drivers). It is
**not** relicensed by this project: it keeps its own MIT license at
[`picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE`](picocalc-text-starter-main/LICENSE),
Copyright © 2025 Blair Leduc. The Raspberry Pi Pico SDK it builds against is
licensed separately by Raspberry Pi Ltd. (BSD-3-Clause).

The vendored copy is unchanged except for **four fixes**:

1. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`, `get_next_free_cluster()` now
   advances its search hint past the cluster it just handed out; without that,
   every later allocation re-scans the clusters already given out, and a long
   sequential write to the SD card looks hung.
2. In the same file, `fat32_dir_read()` skips deleted entries first (an entry marked
   0xE5, whether an 8.3 entry or a long-name part) and checks that a long-name part fits
   the filename buffer; `link_entry()` compares the 0xE5 marker as an unsigned byte.
   Before, a deleted long-name part was read as a live one and wrote 13 bytes at
   `filename + 468` of a 256-byte stack buffer.
3. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/sdcard.c`, the wait for a busy card is timed by
   the clock (0.5 s) and not by counting 10000 bytes, every command except CMD0 waits for
   the card first, and a write returns an error if the card is still busy after it. Without
   it, a card that was still programming a block ignored the next command and reads and
   writes failed on good sectors.

4. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`, `fat32_write()` no longer allocates a cluster twice
   when a write starts exactly at the end of a cluster (one `break` in the loop that walks the chain).
   Before, every such write left one cluster in use that no file owned (28 MB lost on a real card).

Fixes 2 and 3 were sent to the author as pull requests (the patches, standalone tests and
write-ups are in `docs/fat32-pr/`). Fix 4 is prepared as a pull request but not sent yet
(`docs/fat32-pr/PULL-REQUEST-cluster-leak.md`). Everything else is exactly as downloaded.
